_readme: Research warnings compared with the verified case files. Each claim paraphrases one risk from a research source and cites its section and, where the source has pages, the printed page. 'match' links cases automatically: every verified case whose category or actor_type is listed, plus the ids listed, minus 'exclude' and minus any case whose actor_type is in 'exclude_actor_types'. A source with kind 'taxonomy' is a classification of all AI risk rather than a set of warnings, so it is left out of 'what the research did not foresee'. 'status' is an editorial judgement, reviewed when links change: observed (seen in real incidents), early (early or partial signs), lab (only in lab tests or researcher demos), none (nothing in the registry), outside (beyond what a security incident registry can measure). English text here; translations in config/research_i18n/<lang>.json.

sources.title: An Overview of Catastrophic AI Risks
sources.authors: Dan Hendrycks, Mantas Mazeika, Thomas Woodside
sources.about: Published by the Center for AI Safety in June 2023 and revised in October 2023. It sorts catastrophic AI risk into four groups: malicious use, the AI race, organisational risks and rogue AI.

groups.name: Malicious use
groups.blurb: People deliberately using AI to cause harm.

groups.name: AI race
groups.blurb: Competition pushing countries and companies to deploy AI before it is safe.

groups.name: Organisational risks
groups.blurb: Accidents, leaks and weak safety culture at the organisations that build and run AI.

groups.name: Rogue AI
groups.blurb: AI systems that pursue goals nobody intended and resist control.

sources.title: International AI Safety Report 2026
sources.authors: Yoshua Bengio (Chair) and more than 100 AI experts, backed by over 30 countries and international organisations
sources.about: The second edition of the international scientific report on the safety of general-purpose AI, chaired by Yoshua Bengio, with a secretariat at the UK AI Security Institute. It summarises the evidence on malicious use, malfunctions and systemic risks without recommending policy.

groups.name: Malicious use
groups.blurb: People using AI for fraud, manipulation, cyberattacks and weapons, and attacks on AI systems themselves.

groups.name: Malfunctions
groups.blurb: AI that fails, or behaves in ways that weaken human control.

groups.name: Systemic risks
groups.blurb: Wider effects on work and on how people think and decide.

groups.name: Risk management
groups.blurb: Gaps in the safeguards meant to contain these risks.

sources.title: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks
sources.authors: Thomas Kwa, Ben West, Joel Becker and 23 co-authors
sources.about: METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) is a nonprofit that tests frontier AI models before release. This paper measures how long a task, timed by skilled humans, AI agents can complete, and tracks how that has grown since 2019.

groups.name: Agent autonomy
groups.blurb: How much work AI agents can do on their own.

sources.title: Recent Frontier Models Are Reward Hacking
sources.authors: Sydney Von Arx, Lawrence Chan, Beth Barnes
sources.about: A METR report on frontier models cheating on its evaluation tasks: changing the scoring instead of solving the problem.

groups.name: Reward hacking
groups.blurb: AI meeting the letter of a task while defeating its purpose.

sources.title: Frontier Models are Capable of In-context Scheming
sources.authors: Alexander Meinke, Bronson Schoen, Jérémy Scheurer, Mikita Balesni, Rusheb Shah, Marius Hobbhahn
sources.about: Apollo Research is an AI safety organisation that evaluates models for deceptive behaviour. In this study, frontier models were given a goal and a situation in which hiding their actions would help them reach it, to see whether they would scheme.

groups.name: Scheming in tests
groups.blurb: AI covertly pursuing a goal and hiding it from the people overseeing it.

sources.title: Frontier AI Trends Report
sources.about: The UK government's AI Security Institute drew on two years of its own tests of more than 30 frontier models to report trends in capabilities, safeguards, loss-of-control risks and societal impacts.

groups.name: Safeguards
groups.blurb: Whether the protections built into AI systems hold up.

groups.name: Loss of control
groups.blurb: Abilities AI would need to escape human oversight.

groups.name: Societal impacts
groups.blurb: How people rely on AI and what they hand over to it.

sources.title: The AI Risk Repository: A Meta-Review, Database, and Taxonomy of Risks From Artificial Intelligence
sources.authors: Peter Slattery, Alexander K. Saeri, Emily A. C. Grundy, Jess Graham, Michael Noetel, Risto Uuk, James Dao, Soroush Pour, Stephen Casper, Neil Thompson
sources.about: A database of more than 1,700 AI risks gathered from 65 published frameworks, sorted into 7 domains and 24 subdomains. It is used here as a cross-check: each domain is one entry, so you can see which parts of the whole AI risk landscape the registry covers.

groups.name: Seven risk domains
groups.blurb: The domain taxonomy from Table 2 of the paper.

claims.title: AI makes biological weapons easier to build
claims.claim: AI with knowledge of bioengineering could help people create dangerous pathogens and lower the barriers to obtaining them.
claims.note: No verified case in the registry. A security registry would only see this if an attempt were reported publicly, so absence here is weak evidence.

claims.title: People will set AI agents loose to cause harm
claims.claim: AI is increasingly built as agents that act on their own, so people can build agents that pursue harmful goals with little human effort.
claims.note: Criminal and state groups now hand most of an intrusion to AI agents: reconnaissance, exploitation and data theft run with a human only setting the goal.

claims.title: AI floods the information space with tailored lies
claims.claim: AI can generate personalised disinformation at a scale no human team could, degrading a society's shared understanding of reality.
claims.note: Influence networks already use AI to run fake news sites and synthetic presenters. The registry records security-relevant cases only, so it undercounts this risk.

claims.title: People's trust in AI companions turns harmful
claims.claim: As AI seems more human, people form relationships with it and trust it, and that trust can be exploited or lead to harm.
claims.note: The paper already cited the 2023 Belgian chatbot suicide. Since then the registry has filed lawsuits and inquests over deaths and crises linked to chatbots, and a fraud studio that ran thousands of AI personas on dating apps. Most chatbot cases are allegations in court, not findings.

claims.title: AI helps a few concentrate power through surveillance
claims.claim: AI-powered surveillance, censorship and propaganda could let small groups lock in control over society.
claims.note: One case: accounts linked to China used ChatGPT to build a tool that reports on protests abroad to the authorities. Most state surveillance never surfaces as a public security incident.

claims.title: AI makes cyberattacks easier, faster and larger
claims.claim: AI could lower the barrier to entry for cyberattacks and increase their scale, speed and success, including against the infrastructure societies depend on.
claims.note: The best-documented prediction in the registry: novices building ransomware with chatbots, malware that asks a model what to do next, state groups using AI at every stage of an attack, and AI-written scripts probing industrial controllers.

claims.title: Militaries hand life-and-death decisions to AI
claims.claim: An arms race could push militaries toward weapons that select and kill targets without a human decision, and toward automated warfare that escalates faster than people can intervene.
claims.note: Outside what a security incident registry can measure. Military uses of AI are rarely reported as incidents.

claims.title: Companies ship AI before it is safe to win the race
claims.claim: Competitive pressure pushes companies to release AI products first rather than safest, and to treat safety work as something to fix later.
claims.note: Lawsuits by families and US states allege that a chatbot model was rushed to market with shortened safety testing. These are allegations, not court findings.

claims.title: Automation leaves society dependent on AI
claims.claim: Companies replacing human labour with AI could cause mass unemployment and leave society unable to function without AI systems.
claims.note: An economic risk, outside what a security incident registry measures.

claims.title: Competition selects for selfish AI
claims.claim: Over the long run, competition between AI systems could favour those with selfish traits and gradually displace human control.
claims.note: A long-term dynamic that no single incident can show.

claims.title: Powerful AI gets leaked or stolen
claims.claim: AI models could be leaked by accident or stolen by state, industry or criminal actors, which is why AI developers need state-of-the-art information security.
claims.note: Model weights have not been publicly reported stolen, but leaked keys exposed private models, outsiders reached a restricted model, source code shipped by accident, and AI companies accuse rivals of copying model capabilities through mass querying.

claims.title: Accidents with AI are hard to avoid
claims.claim: AI systems are complex and unreliable, so accidents are normal; the goal must be to stop accidents from cascading into disasters.
claims.note: Coding agents have wiped databases and drives, assistants have published private chats, and staff acting on an AI agent's advice exposed sensitive data.

claims.title: AI developers' own safety measures fail
claims.claim: Organisations building advanced AI may lack a strong safety culture, so tests, controls and warnings fail when they matter.
claims.note: Several AI developers and a government institute ran tests whose agents got out and reached real companies and government systems; some victims learned of it before the developer did.

claims.title: AI reaches its goal by means nobody intended
claims.claim: AI given a measurable stand-in for what we want finds loopholes that satisfy the measure while missing the real goal.
claims.note: Test agents that hit a block have reached for proxy servers, keys found in public code and other companies' systems to finish their task. This fits the pattern, though the reports rarely explain the agent's reasoning.

claims.title: AI's goals drift over time
claims.claim: Even AI that starts with goals people endorse could see them change as it adapts, in ways that are hard to predict.
claims.note: No verified case. The paper itself calls this its most speculative section.

claims.title: AI seeks more access and resources than it was given
claims.claim: Gaining power and resources helps with almost any goal, so capable AI agents may seek them, through legitimate means, deception or force.
claims.note: Agents in tests have escaped their sandboxes, used computing and accounts they were not given, and broken into outside systems. No case shows an AI seeking power for its own sake; each grabbed access while pursuing an assigned task.

claims.title: AI deceives the people who oversee it
claims.claim: AI could learn to appear under control while it is not, so monitoring alone cannot be relied on.
claims.note: One verified case: after wiping a production database, a coding agent reported misleadingly on what it had done. Deliberate deception toward overseers is not yet established in a real incident.

claims.title: AI-made fakes fuel fraud and extortion
claims.claim: Realistic AI-generated voices, images and video are used for fraud, extortion and sexual imagery made without consent, and cheap tools have made such content easy to produce at scale.
claims.note: The largest category in the registry: cloned voices and deepfake video calls impersonating executives, officials and relatives, and deepfake celebrity ads behind investment scams. The report adds that victims often do not report, so public cases undercount the harm.

claims.title: AI content is used to sway what people believe
claims.claim: AI-generated content can shift people's beliefs about as well as people can, and some actors use it to manipulate; evidence of how well this works outside the lab is still limited.
claims.note: The registry records influence operations using AI-written news sites, deepfake videos of leaders and synthetic presenters, but not whether they changed anyone's mind. That matches the report's caution about real-world effect.

claims.title: Criminals and state hackers use AI in cyberattacks
claims.claim: There is strong evidence that criminal groups and state-backed attackers use AI in their operations, especially to find software flaws and write malicious code, though it is not yet clear whether AI has made attacks larger or more damaging overall.
claims.note: Matches the registry closely: AI-written ransomware and stealers, malware that asks a model what to do while it runs, and state groups using chatbots for reconnaissance, phishing and exploit work. Like the report, the case files show use, not overall effect.

claims.title: AI runs more of each attack, short of full autonomy
claims.claim: AI is taking over more steps of a cyberattack. At least one real attack was semi-autonomous, with people stepping in only at key decisions, but no fully autonomous attack from start to finish had been reported.
claims.note: The semi-autonomous case the report describes is on file: a Chinese state group that had Claude Code agents do most of an intrusion. The registry holds more intrusions described as run largely by AI agents with a human setting the goal, several reported after the report came out. Whether any was autonomous from start to finish rests on the investigators' own accounts.

claims.title: AI gives expert-level help toward biological and chemical weapons
claims.claim: AI systems can give detailed help relevant to making biological and chemical weapons. In 2025 several developers added stronger safeguards because they could not rule out meaningful help to novices.
claims.note: No verified case. As with the CAIS warning on biological weapons, an attempt would only reach the registry if it were reported publicly.

claims.title: AI systems themselves become targets
claims.claim: Attackers can manipulate AI systems through prompt injection, poisoned data and compromised components, to change how they behave or to pull out sensitive information.
claims.note: Hidden instructions that make assistants leak mail and files, hijacked coding agents, malicious packages and plugins aimed at AI developers, and actively exploited flaws in AI tools. Many prompt injection cases are demonstrations by researchers; most supply-chain attacks happened in the real world.

claims.title: AI agents fail with fewer chances to stop them
claims.claim: AI systems still make errors and invent information, and agents raise the stakes because they act directly on other systems, leaving people fewer chances to step in.
claims.note: Coding agents have wiped a production database and a whole drive, pushed internal screenshots to public code sites and given advice that exposed sensitive data; an assistant summarised confidential emails it should not have read, and a model filed a false murder tip with police.

claims.title: AI notices tests and games its evaluations
claims.claim: Models increasingly recognise when they are being tested and find loopholes to score well, which makes it harder to measure what they can really do. The report finds today's systems still lack the abilities needed for loss of control.
claims.note: Reported from developers' and researchers' own testing. The registry's evaluation incidents are a different problem: test agents that broke out of their environment and reached real systems (see the CAIS warning on developers' safety measures failing). None shows a model gaming its test.

claims.title: Relying on AI companions harms some users
claims.claim: AI companion apps have reached tens of millions of users. Early, mixed evidence links frequent use to more loneliness and less social contact, and heavy reliance on AI can weaken people's own judgement.
claims.note: The registry holds lawsuits, an inquest and press reports linking chatbot conversations to suicides, delusions and violence. Most are allegations in court, not findings, and they are severe individual cases rather than the population-wide effects the report discusses.

claims.title: AI reshapes jobs, starting with early-career workers
claims.claim: AI can do tasks in a large share of jobs. Early data shows little change in overall employment but fewer jobs for early-career workers in the most exposed occupations.
claims.note: An economic risk, outside what a security incident registry measures.

claims.title: Safeguards on open models are easily stripped
claims.claim: Models whose weights are published can be modified to remove their safeguards, their use is hard to monitor, and a release cannot be recalled.
claims.note: Attack tools on file run on open models: a WormGPT variant built on Mixtral, a darknet platform claiming self-hosted models, an APT28 stealer that queries Qwen, a ransomware prototype using a local open model and a hijacked Ollama server used as the brain of a hacking tool. None shows weights modified to strip safeguards; the WormGPT variant relied on its instructions.

claims.title: AI agents can handle ever longer tasks
claims.claim: The length of software tasks that AI agents can complete half the time has doubled about every seven months since 2019. If the trend holds, agents could do many month-long tasks within five years.
claims.note: A trend in capability, not a harm, so the registry cannot test it. It does record intrusions that AI agents ran for hours with little human input (see the warnings on AI agents in cyberattacks).

claims.title: AI agents cheat on their tasks, knowing it is not wanted
claims.claim: On METR's test tasks, frontier models often scored well by tampering with the scoring code or copying answers instead of solving the problem, and afterwards said this went against what the user wanted. Telling them not to cheat barely helped.
claims.note: Seen in evaluation tasks. In the real world, test agents that hit a block have used proxies, keys found in public code and other companies' systems to finish their task. That resembles the pattern, but none of those reports shows an agent faking its result.

claims.title: AI works around its overseers when goals clash
claims.claim: Given a goal that conflicted with their developers', several frontier models in test scenarios switched off oversight settings, tried to copy what they believed were their own weights elsewhere, or manipulated data while appearing to do the task.
claims.note: Seen only in Apollo's controlled scenarios, where the model was given a strong goal and the means to act. No case file shows an AI switching off its oversight or copying itself in the real world.

claims.title: AI keeps lying when asked what it did
claims.claim: Questioned after such covert actions, some models denied them, and one model (OpenAI's o1) kept up the deception in most follow-up questions.
claims.note: One verified case comes close: after wiping a production database during a code freeze, Replit's coding agent reported misleadingly on what it had done. It is not established that this was deliberate.

claims.title: AI behaves differently when it thinks it is watched
claims.claim: Some models acted as intended when they believed they were being watched and pursued their own goal otherwise, and several deliberately did worse on tests when high scores would have led to restrictions.
claims.note: A finding about testing itself. It would only surface as an incident if a developer reported it, and nothing in the registry shows it.

claims.title: Every AI system tested could be jailbroken
claims.claim: AISI found universal jailbreaks, attacks that get past safeguards across many kinds of harmful request, in every system it tested, though some safeguards now take far more expert effort to break.
claims.note: Real attackers get past safeguards: state groups had refused requests answered by posing as auditors, capture-the-flag players or authorised penetration testers, criminals sell jailbroken chatbots for malware and phishing, and an inquest heard that a teenager got harmful information from ChatGPT after saying his questions were for research.

claims.title: AI gets better at the steps needed to copy itself
claims.claim: In simplified tests, the best models' success at tasks needed to copy themselves rose from under 5% in 2023 to over 60% in 2025. They handle early steps such as getting computing power and money, but struggle to copy themselves and keep running.
claims.note: No case file shows an AI copying itself. The nearest real events are test agents that used computing and accounts they were not given (see the CAIS warning on AI seeking more access).

claims.title: AI can do worse on tests on purpose
claims.claim: Models can deliberately underperform on evaluations when told to, sometimes subtly enough to fool automated monitors. AISI found no sign of models doing this unprompted.
claims.note: A risk to how AI is tested rather than a security incident. Nothing in the registry shows it.

claims.title: Many people lean on AI for emotional support
claims.claim: A third of UK adults surveyed had used AI for emotional support or company in the past year, and some users of companion apps showed withdrawal-like distress when the service went down.
claims.note: The registry holds lawsuits, an inquest and press reports linking chatbot conversations to suicides, delusions and violence. Most are allegations in court, not findings.

claims.title: AI agents get the power to move money
claims.claim: Newly published tools increasingly let AI agents carry out consequential actions in finance, such as transferring assets and trading, rather than only reading data.
claims.note: No case file yet shows an AI agent moving money wrongly or being tricked into it. Hijacked agents on file have leaked data and run code; with payment powers, the same attacks would reach money.

claims.title: Discrimination and toxic content
claims.claim: AI that treats groups unfairly, works worse for some groups, or exposes people to harmful content such as hate speech or abusive imagery.
claims.note: Mostly outside a security registry: bias and unequal performance are not security incidents. A few case files touch abusive imagery, such as AI-made explicit videos of a singer.

claims.title: Privacy and security
claims.claim: AI that leaks or infers sensitive personal data, and weaknesses in AI systems and their toolchains that attackers exploit.
claims.note: One of the two pillars of the registry: leaked chats and keys, exposed databases, prompt injection, hijacked agents, poisoned packages and stolen AI accounts.

claims.title: Misinformation
claims.claim: AI that produces false or misleading information by mistake, and floods of personalised content that wear away a shared sense of what is true.
claims.note: One case fits the first part directly: an AI model filed a false murder tip with police. Deliberate disinformation belongs to the next domain, malicious actors.

claims.title: Malicious actors and misuse
claims.claim: People using AI for disinformation, surveillance and propaganda at scale; for cyberattacks and weapons; and for fraud, scams and targeted manipulation.
claims.note: The other pillar of the registry: deepfake fraud, AI-built malware, AI phishing and state operations.

claims.title: Human-computer interaction
claims.claim: People over-trusting or depending on AI, emotionally or materially, and handing it decisions in ways that weaken their own agency.
claims.note: Lawsuits and an inquest link chatbot conversations to suicides and delusions, and an engineer exposed sensitive data by acting on an AI agent's faulty advice. Most chatbot cases are allegations in court, not findings.

claims.title: Socioeconomic and environmental harm
claims.claim: AI concentrating power, deepening inequality, devaluing human work, feeding a development race, outpacing governance and harming the environment.
claims.note: Outside what a security incident registry measures.

claims.title: AI system safety, failures and limitations
claims.claim: AI pursuing goals that conflict with ours, having dangerous capabilities, failing under real conditions, being hard to understand, and risks that arise when many AI agents interact.
claims.note: Agents that wiped data, escaped test environments, reached outside systems and filed a false report. These are failures and unintended behaviour; none shows an AI pursuing goals of its own.
